To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) the adversarially trained models we study are more robust than their non-adversarially trained counterparts; 2) adversarially trained CNNs are more robust to natural corruptions than to adversarial attacks; 3) adversarially robust CNNs tend to have a shape and simplicity bias, and 4) adversarially training a CNN on the ImageNet dataset does not necessarily make the model robust to natural corrup-tions.

(i) adversarially robust models are biased towards simple and regular shapes, which can be seen by their higher classification accuracy on CIFAR10, a dataset that is known to contain more simple shapes than ImageNet; (ii) adversarially trained models are biased towards the shape prior of ImageNet, and the shape prior of CIFAR10, but not towards the shape prior learned by the same model during training on CIFAR10.

1) the shape and simplicity biases are present in adversarially trained models, and 2) these biases are not a byproduct of the optimization process, but are instead the result of the adversarial training procedure.

the following: 1) the effect of adversarial training on the shape bias of CNNs; 2) the impact of the shape bias on adversarially trained models; and 3) whether we can mitigate the adversarial robustness- shape bias trade-off

adversarially trained models are not as robust as we thought, especially when they are trained on large datasets like ImageNet.
